prompt: A commuter coffee shop launches a mobile pre-order app. Name which component of TAM each customer statement shows.

cases.text: Ordering on the train saves me ten minutes every morning before work.
cases.explanation: Perceived Usefulness (PU) is the belief that using the technology enhances performance or productivity by saving time.

cases.text: Reordering my usual latte takes two taps and no typing at all.
cases.explanation: Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) is the belief that using the technology will be free of effort.

cases.text: I really like having this app on my phone. It is a great way to buy coffee.
cases.explanation: Attitude Toward Use is the overall favorable or unfavorable feeling determined by usefulness and ease of use.

cases.text: Starting Monday, I am going to pre-order through the app every commute.
cases.explanation: Behavioral Intention to Use is the plan to use the technology in future activities.

cases.text: Finding the oat-milk option takes way too many menus and buried settings.
cases.explanation: Effort and friction in the interface directly lower Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU).

question_text: An online electronics retailer adds twelve new comparison filters, live voice commands, and a warranty calculator into a single chat window for its virtual shopping assistant. Customers suddenly stop finishing their chats. According to the TAM analysis for BestBuy, what best explains this drop?
hint: Consider the slide's question on how adding more features affects ease of use.
correct_answer_citation: How is adding more features reducing the ease of use?

options.option_text: Packing too many features into the interface reduced Perceived Ease of Use, hurting customers' attitude and intention to use the assistant.
options.option_explanation: Right. Even features meant to be helpful can clutter the chat interface and lower Perceived Ease of Use, which dampens attitude toward using and actual adoption.

options.option_text: According to TAM, adding features always increases both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness.
options.option_explanation: Adding features may aim to raise usefulness, but it often increases complexity and reduces Perceived Ease of Use.

options.option_text: Perceived Ease of Use has no effect on Attitude Toward Using once a customer visits an e-commerce site.
options.option_explanation: In TAM, both Perceived Usefulness and Perceived Ease of Use determine Attitude Toward Using.

options.option_text: Online reviews and influencer endorsements directly determine Actual System Use without affecting usefulness or ease of use.
options.option_explanation: In TAM, social influence acts as an external variable that shapes Perceived Usefulness and Perceived Ease of Use first.

prompt: A regional clinic rolls out an AI symptom-checker chatbot. Sort each item into External Variables, TAM Beliefs (Ease of Use & Usefulness), or Benefits for the Hospital.

cards.text: Natural language processing connected to verified medical databases
cards.explanation: System features (NLP and medical databases) are an external variable.

cards.text: Local family doctors and community leaders endorse the chatbot to patients
cards.explanation: Social influence from healthcare professionals and community leaders is an external variable.

cards.text: Patients can describe symptoms in everyday, non-technical language
cards.explanation: Handling non-technical language with a simple interface creates Perceived Ease of Use.

cards.text: Nurses see that the tool filters out minor colds so they can treat critical cases
cards.explanation: Filtering non-urgent cases so staff can focus on critical patients is Perceived Usefulness.

cards.text: Patients receive quicker responses and clearer guidance for their symptoms
cards.explanation: Improved patient experience is one of the three measured benefits for the hospital.

cards.text: Shorter triage times allow the clinic to allocate beds and staff more efficiently
cards.explanation: Operational efficiency and better resource allocation are hospital-level benefits of adoption.

prompt: A hardware store introduces a self-return kiosk. Put the customer's adoption journey in the order of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM).

steps.text: The store sets up a touch-screen kiosk with a barcode scanner, on-screen guidance, and a staff member nearby.
steps.explanation: 1. External Variables: system features and training/support come first outside the core beliefs.

steps.text: A shopper notices the step-by-step visual prompts look effortless and that using the kiosk skips the twenty-minute counter queue.
steps.explanation: 2. Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness are shaped by those external variables.

steps.text: Because it looks both simple and time-saving, the shopper views the kiosk as an effective solution.
steps.explanation: 3. Attitude Toward Using (A) is determined by Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness.

steps.text: The shopper decides to use the kiosk for next week's return and tells a neighbor to try it too.
steps.explanation: 4. Behavioral Intention to Use (BI) follows from a positive attitude.

steps.text: Over the season, shoppers routinely complete returns at the kiosk, cutting counter lines and freeing staff for complex issues.
steps.explanation: 5. Actual System Use is the final outcome, producing operational efficiency and cost savings.

prompt: A law firm rolls out a new document-search platform. Match each primary UTAUT construct with what it captures at the firm.

pairs.match: Associates believe the platform lets them find case precedents in half the time.
pairs.explanation: Performance Expectancy is how much the technology is perceived to enhance job performance.

pairs.match: Paralegals find the search bar and filters straightforward to learn on day one.
pairs.explanation: Effort Expectancy reflects the perceived ease of use of the technology.

pairs.match: Senior partners openly expect every practice group to use the new platform.
pairs.explanation: Social Influence is how much individuals perceive that important others believe they should use the technology.

pairs.match: The firm provides fast Wi-Fi, a Lunch-and-Learn workshop, and a dedicated helpdesk.
pairs.explanation: Facilitating Conditions are the infrastructure, training, and technical support available to users.

prompt: An airline installs self-service bag-drop kiosks at its terminals. Name which moderating variable from the IKEA UTAUT analysis explains each pattern.

cases.text: When the airline closes all staffed desks so flyers feel forced to use the kiosk, satisfaction scores drop sharply.
cases.explanation: Voluntariness of Use: when customers feel forced to use the kiosk with no alternative, satisfaction and adoption are impacted.

cases.text: Travelers who have used self-check-in machines at hotels and train stations breeze through without asking staff for help.
cases.explanation: Experience: prior familiarity with similar technologies helps users adapt faster with less guidance.

cases.text: University students on spring break adopt the touch-screen tag printers almost immediately compared with older flyers.
cases.explanation: Age: younger customers often adopt the kiosk more quickly due to greater familiarity with technology.

cases.text: Airports in regions where automated train gates and self-checkout are everyday norms see twice the first-month kiosk usage.
cases.explanation: Cultural Context: acceptance varies with regional or cultural familiarity with self-service technology.

prompt: A hospital deploys connected patient-monitoring wristbands. Match each IoT privacy and security best practice with how the hospital applies it.

pairs.match: Replace factory passwords with digital certificates and two-factor sign-in for nurse tablets.
pairs.explanation: Strong authentication uses two-factor authentication, biometrics, or digital certificates instead of default passwords.

pairs.match: Encrypt wristband traffic with TLS/SSL and place medical sensors on a separate network segment.
pairs.explanation: Securing network communications means encrypting data in transit and segmenting IoT devices on separate networks.

pairs.match: Turn on automatic security patching so every wristband receives firmware fixes overnight.
pairs.explanation: Regularly updating firmware and enabling automatic updates protects against known vulnerabilities.

pairs.match: Record only pulse and temperature needed for care, and pseudonymize patient identifiers.
pairs.explanation: Collecting only the minimum necessary data and anonymizing or pseudonymizing it reduces breach impact.

pairs.match: Train ward staff on safe device setup and how to report unusual sensor alerts immediately.
pairs.explanation: Educating users provides clear guidelines on setup, use, and reporting suspicious activities.

prompt: A cold-chain logistics company installs connected temperature sensors in its refrigerated trucks. Put the five stages of the IoT Device Management Process in order.

steps.text: Provisioning and Authentication: register each new truck sensor and verify its cryptographic identity on the network.
steps.explanation: 1. Provisioning and Authentication comes first when enrolling new devices.

steps.text: Configuration and Control: set the temperature alert thresholds and sampling intervals remotely for each route.
steps.explanation: 2. Configuration and Control sets how authenticated devices operate.

steps.text: Monitoring and Diagnostics: track sensor battery levels, signal strength, and fault logs while trucks are on the road.
steps.explanation: 3. Monitoring and Diagnostics watches active devices in real time to catch issues.

steps.text: Software Updates and Maintenance: push a firmware patch over the air to fix a calibration bug across the fleet.
steps.explanation: 4. Software Updates and Maintenance keeps deployed devices secure and reliable.

steps.text: Decommissioning: revoke network credentials and wipe stored logs when an old sensor unit is retired.

prompt: A manufacturing group connects its factories and delivery fleet. Name whether each part of its architecture is IoT, Edge, Fog, or Cloud.

cases.text: Smart thermostats and vibration sensors mounted on assembly-line motors that collect and transmit readings.
cases.explanation: IoT refers to connected physical devices that collect and transmit data from their environment.

cases.text: An onboard processor inside an autonomous forklift that stops the vehicle in milliseconds when a person steps in front of it.
cases.explanation: Edge computing processes data right at or near the source for ultra-low-latency, real-time tasks.

cases.text: A local factory-floor network node that aggregates machine readings across one plant and sends hourly summaries upstream.
cases.explanation: Fog computing acts as a bridge between edge and cloud, analyzing machine data across local networks before sending summaries to the cloud.

cases.text: A centralized remote data center on AWS that stores five years of global sales and production history for company-wide analytics.
cases.explanation: Cloud computing provides centralized storage and processing over the internet with high scalability.
